faculty_id.title: Trust in Artificial Intelligence
faculty_id.description: Building trust in AI systems and technologies is critical for our future. Drawing on my extensive research into the subject, I will highlight key insights from our multi-country survey to answer questions ranging from whether people trust in AI systems, to the expectations of its governance and use, and what can be done to support community trust in AI. Our research also highlights several pathways to enhancing trust and acceptance of AI systems. I will conclude this module with an introduction to the business model and practical guidelines on achieving trustworthy AI, which we developed as part of our research.
faculty_id.short_description: Drawing on her extensive research into the subject, Professor Gillespie highlights key insights from her multicountry survey about trust in AI.

faculty_junction_id.name: Nicole Gillespie
faculty_junction_id.title: KPMG Chair in Organisational Trust & Professor in Management & KPMG Chair in Trust School of Business
faculty_junction_id.bio:
Trained as an organizational psychologist, Nicole’s research focuses on trust development and repair in organisational contexts, and in contexts where trust is challenged (e.g. after a trust failure, in complex stakeholder environments, during organizational transformation and digital disruption, in emerging technologies and virtual healthcare, in cross-cultural relations). Current research projects focus on understanding stakeholder trust in organizations and industries, organizational trust repair, designing trustworthy organizations, trust in Artificial Intelligence and emerging technologies, and stakeholder trust and uptake of telemedicine. Her research appears in leading international journals, including the Academy of Management Review, Journal of Management, Journal of Applied Psychology, Organization Studies, Accounting Organizations and Society, European Journal of Information Systems, Journal of Services Research, Business Ethics Quarterly, Journal of Business Ethics, Human Resource Management, Sloan Management Review and Work and Stress, as well as in books and book chapters. She has also published in a range of health journals including Lancet Digital Health, Journal of Telemedicine and Telecare, Digital Health, and Dermatology. Her work has been extensively presented in Europe, the USA and Australia. She is Deputy Editor of the Journal of Trust Research and on the editorial board of the leading leadership journal, Leadership Quarterly.

Nicole has written commissioned research reports and case studies on building and repairing stakeholder trust for the UK Institute of Business Ethics, the World Economic Forum, and a policy note for the UK Parliament on restoring trust in the financial sector after the global financial crisis. Her most recent reports in collaboration with KPMG are Trustworthy by Design: A practical guide to organisational trust ; Trust in Artificial Intelligence: Australian Insights 2020 ; and Achieving Trustworthy AI: A model for trustworthy artificial intelligence. Her research and consulting has led to positive changes in industry, government and policy across a range of sectors, including Health, Resources, Finance and Banking, Higher Education, R&D, Not-for-Profit and the Defence industry. Clients include KPMG, the World Economic Forum, the Ontario Hospital Association, Barclays Bank, UBS Bank, Royal Brisbane and Women’s Hospital, the Royal Flying Doctor Service, CSIRO, The Australian Army, Bank of Queensland, Santos, Origin Energy and various government agencies. She has attracted over $7million in research funding as a Chief Investigator with her colleagues, including ARC, NHMRC and industry grants. Nicole is an active member of the Academy of Management, the European Group of Organisational Studies, and the First International Network on Trust and sits on multiple Advisory Boards.

Nicole has over twenty years experience in designing and delivering MBA, Executive MBA, specialist masters and undergraduate courses. She is the recipient of five teaching excellence awards and, together with former PhD student Mattia Anesa, two best paper awards from the Academy of Management. She is the recipient of the 2016 UQ Business School Research Award. In 2019 she was made a Fellow of the Australian and New Zealand School of Government in recognition of outstanding contribution to public management.
faculty_junction_id.short_bio: Nicole Gillespie is the KPMG Chair in Organizational Trust and Professor of Management at the University of Queensland Business School, and an International Research Fellow at the Centre for Corporate Reputation, Oxford University. She co-leads the Trust, Ethics and Governance Alliance at the University of Queensland. Nicole joined UQ Business School in January 2010. Prior to this she held faculty and research positions at Melbourne Business School, Warwick Business School (UK), The Australian & New Zealand School of Government, The University of Melbourne, University of Queensland, and Swinburne University of Technology.

faculty_id.title: Indigenous Data Sovereignty
faculty_id.description: Indigenous data is data, information, and knowledge in any format that impacts Indigenous Peoples, nations, and communities at the collective and individual level. This course unpacks the idea of indigenous data sovereignty, and associated principles, frameworks, challenges. Professor Hudson also discusses Maori approaches to Artificial Intelligence and what it means to indigenize AI.
faculty_id.short_description: This course unpacks the idea of indigenous data sovereignty, and associated principles, frameworks, challenges. Professor Hudson also discusses Maori approaches to Artificial Intelligence and what it means to indigenize AI.

faculty_junction_id.name: Maui Hudson
faculty_junction_id.title: Associate Professor and Director, Te Kotahi Research Institute
faculty_junction_id.bio: Access to data and governance of data are key issues emerging from his research and led to his involvement in the establishment of Te Mana Raraunga, the Māori Data Sovereignty Network, and the Global Indigenous Data Alliance. He is the Co-Director of ENRICH, a collaboration between NYU and University of Waikato, and a Co-Director of Local Contexts, a system which digitally tags Indigenous interests in traditional knowledge and biodata.
faculty_junction_id.short_bio: Maui affiliates to Te Whakatohea, Nga Ruahine, and Te Mahurehure iwi and is currently the deputy chair of the Whakatohea Māori Trust Board. Maui is an Associate Professor and Director of the Te Kotahi Research Institute at the University of Waikato. His research is interdisciplinary in nature focusing on the application of mātauranga Māori (indigenous knowledge) to decision-making across a range of contexts from new technologies to health, the environment to innovation.

faculty_id.title: AI Ethics in the LAC Region
faculty_id.description: People tend to focus on the United States, the European Union and China when thinking about artificial intelligence, ignoring innovative developments in AI technologies for the public sector emerging from the LAC region. Pombo discusses numerous efforts Latin American and Caribbean countries are making to promote the responsible use of AI. She also shares a few examples of creative uses of AI technologies to address challenges unique to the LAC region. The module concludes with an overview of the tools developed by the Inter-American Development Bank’s fAIr LAC initiative that help bring ethical AI principles into practice.
faculty_id.short_description: This module walks the audience through the state of the AI and ethics ecosystem in Latin America and the Caribbean.

faculty_junction_id.name: Cristina Pombo
faculty_junction_id.title: Principal Advisor, Head of the Digital and Data Cluster, Social Sector Department
faculty_junction_id.short_bio: Cristina is an economist with an emphasis on social policy working in the intersection of technology and government, ethics & AI. She advises the Manager and Division Chiefs of the Inter-American Development Bank´s Social Sector on operational issues and digital transformation strategies in education, health, social protection, labor markets, gender, diversity, and migration. In this capacity, she spearheads initiatives that leverage digital technologies to improve social services such as fAIr LAC, the first public-private alliance for a responsible use of artificial intelligence in the region. She is part of the OECD Network of Experts on AI. Expert in Digital Transformation in Governments from the Harvard Kennedy School and in Data Ethics from the University of Michigan.

faculty_id.title: Algorithmic Transparency in the Public Sector
faculty_id.description: Drawing on her professional experience working on data ethics, open data and open government, Domagala explains the concept of algorithmic transparency and why is is a critical need in our society today. She shares different examples of algorithmic transparency measures from Europe and North America with a special focus on the UK’s new Algorithmic Transparency Standard. She concludes her module with an outlook on the field of algorithmic transparency over the next few years and suggestions on what actors in the field ought to focus on going forward.
faculty_id.short_description: In this module, Domagala explains the need for algorithmic transparency in our society today and shares examples of new measures from Europe and North America.

faculty_junction_id.name: Natalia Domagala
faculty_junction_id.title: Head of Data Ethics
faculty_junction_id.bio: She previously advised on open government and open data policies for the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport in the UK, and implemented open data challenges for 360Giving. She has research experience in anthropology, gender, civic tech, and economic development, and she has recently co-edited a book: Situating Open Data: Global Trends in Local Contexts. Natalia is a Policy Fellow at the Centre for Science and Policy, University of Cambridge. She received her MSc in Local Economic Development from the London School of Economics and Political Science and her BA in Anthropology and Media from Goldsmiths, University of London.
faculty_junction_id.short_bio: Natalia Domagala leads on data ethics policy at the Central Digital and Data Office, Cabinet Office in the UK.

faculty_id.title: AI Ethics: Autonomous Driving
faculty_id.description: The development and implementation of autonomous vehicles is rising fast, while the scrutiny of some ethical issues fall behind. Therefore, this course module gives an overview of key ethical considerations relating to autonomous driving. In particular, the course will elaborate on the Trolley Problem, a thought experiment that has dominated the scientific debate in the field of autonomous driving ethics in the past. It will be highlighted why a move away from this concept and towards the ethics of risks is necessary and will introduce a first approach of doing so. Furthermore, the course will summarize some ethical recommendations that were developed by expert groups for industry and policymakers in the automotive sector. Lastly, the course will sketch the current status of legal frameworks.
faculty_id.short_description: In this module, Professor Lütge provides an overview of key ethical considerations relating to autonomous driving. He discusses the Trolley Problem, the ethics of risk and ethical recommendations from the automotive industry.

faculty_junction_id.organization: TUM Institute for Ethics in Artificial Intelligence (IEAI)
faculty_junction_id.name: Christoph Lütge (Course Lead)
faculty_junction_id.title: Director
faculty_junction_id.bio:
Professor Lütge has a background both in philosophy as well as business informatics, having taken his PhD at the Technical University of Braunschweig in 1999 and his habilitation at the University of Munich (LMU) in 2005. In 2007, he was awarded a Heisenberg Fellowship by the German Research Foundation. His most recent books are: “An Introduction to Ethics in Robotics and AI” (Springer, 2021, with coauthors) and “Business Ethics: An Economically Informed Perspective” (Oxford University Press, 2021, with Matthias Uhl). He is a member of the European AI Ethics initiative AI4People and of the German Ethics Commission on Automated and Connected Driving (2016-17).

Since 2020, he is Consortium Leader of the Global AI Ethics Consortium.
faculty_junction_id.short_bio: Christoph Lütge is Full Professor of Business Ethics at Technical University of Munich (TUM) and the Director of the TUM Institute for Ethics in Artificial Intelligence (IEAI). He is Distinguished Visiting Professor of Tokyo University and has held further visiting positions at Harvard, Stockholm, Taipei and Kyoto. He has been appointed as an External Member of the Karel Čapek Center for Values in Science and Technology of the Czech Academy of Sciences, Prague, as well as of the Executive Committee of the International Society of Business, Economics, and Ethics (ISBEE).

faculty_id.title: Discrimination in an Automated Society: Contributions from Latin America
faculty_id.description: Do current Latin American laws protect people against discrimination due to the use of automated decision-making by artificial intelligence? How should an effective legal framework on this matter be configured? Based on these questions, this lecture analyzes this type of discrimination from the technical and regulatory point of view, provides a conceptual theory on the particularities of algorithmic discrimination situated and contextualized in Latin America, proposes the adoption of a relational principle based on a philosophical perspective, present in all Latin American indigenous peoples, and offer a new interpretive approach to the principle of equality and the concept of discrimination under a collective view, in order to overcome normative challenges evidenced in comparative law.
faculty_id.short_description: Do current Latin American laws protect people against discrimination due to the use of automated decision-making by AI? This module unpacks this question and considers legal frameworks to mitigate this challenge in the context of automated societies in Latin America.

faculty_junction_id.name: Catherine Muñoz
faculty_junction_id.title: Director and Founding Member, OptIA and Director
faculty_junction_id.bio:
She is the director and a founding member of the Chilean NGO OptIA, the first Observatory for Algorithmic Transparency and Inclusion in Latin America. For the past 4 years, Catherine has worked as a consultant in public policy, with a focus on the social impacts of artificial intelligence systems and their regulation. She also serves as the director of Idónea IA, a legal technology consulting firm that works on risk mitigation and regulatory frameworks to promote ethical and responsible technological innovation.

Catherine has a Bachelor of Laws in Legal and Social Sciences from the Central University of Chile, a Master of Laws in International Law from Heidelberg University, and a Master of Laws in International Law Investments, Trade and Arbitration from the University of Chile. She is a member of the Global AI Ethics Consortium.
faculty_junction_id.short_bio: Catherine Muñoz is an Chilean lawyer specialising in intellectual property, technology, AI ethics and regulation. She has over 10 years of experience in the field of intellectual property and technology regulation with a strong foundation in international treaties related to trade, technology and human rights.

faculty_id.title: Ethical Ambiguities of our Emergent Digital World
faculty_id.description: In this module, Naudé approaches the question of ethical AI from a more philosophical standpoint. He puts forth three broad ethical questions: Does technology increase inequality? Does technology decrease human autonomy? Does technology provide a sense-making narrative? Through the use of major philosophical teachings from the likes of Kant, Descartes and Feuerbach, as well as application-based cases, Naudé walks the audience through each question and presents his findings.
faculty_id.short_description: In this module, Naudé approaches the question of ethical AI from a more philosophical standpoint.

faculty_junction_id.name: Piet Naudé
faculty_junction_id.title: Professor of Ethics
faculty_junction_id.bio: His academic background is in Philosophy and Theology and he specializes in ethics methodology and applied ethics with a global perspective. His most recent book, Contemporary Management Education: Eight questions that will shape its future in the 21st century (Springer 2022) is an ethical perspective on business school education, and includes a dedicated chapter on technology.
faculty_junction_id.short_bio: Piet Naudé is immediate past Director and Professor of Ethics at University of Stellenbosch Business School, South Africa.

faculty_id.title: Implementing Responsible AI
faculty_id.description: This module introduces the audience to the concept of responsible AI and the many factors that play a role in the design, development, deployment and use of responsible AI systems. It outlines key challenges and explains how different stakeholders may take different approaches in their mitigation strategies. This module also looks at the work the Responsible AI Institute (RAII) is doing in the field and on the creation of their formal certification system for responsible AI systems.
faculty_id.short_description: This module introduces us to the concept of responsible AI and look at the factors that play a role in the design, development, deployment and use of responsible AI systems.

faculty_junction_id.name: Ashley Casovan
faculty_junction_id.title: Executive Director
faculty_junction_id.bio: Ashley currently serves as the Executive Director of the Responsible AI Institute (RAII), a multi-stakeholder non-profit dedicated to mitigating harm and unintended consequences of AI systems. RAII’s current objective is completing the architecture for the world’s first independent, accredited certification for responsible AI systems. Previously, Ashley served as the Director of Data and Digital for the Government of Canada, where she led the development of the first national government policy for responsible AI. Her work and ability to bring experts together to solve important challenges have led to meaningful change in government and industry.
faculty_junction_id.short_bio: Ashley is a recognized technology policy expert who has dedicated her career to ensuring data and technology are used in a manner that protects the public. Primarily working in the public sector, her experience lies at the intersection of responsible AI governance, standards, and data governance. Ashley’s ultimate mission is to provide safe, responsible technology that is equitable and safe for all.

faculty_id.title: The Journey towards Responsible AI
faculty_id.description: In this module, we are introduced to the origins of responsible AI and learn about organizational approaches to responsible AI. The module walks us through five rules to enable an organization to have a smoother and more successful journey towards responsible AI. While these rules generally focus on the product level, they have implications for organizational levels as well and offer key insights into building effective and empowered teams in this field. The module concludes with key learnings from Axente’s experience in the revolution that is responsible AI both at PwC and at client organizations.
faculty_id.short_description: In this module, we are introduced to the origins of responsible AI and learn about organizational approaches to responsible AI.

faculty_junction_id.name: Maria Luciana Axente
faculty_junction_id.title: Responsible AI Lead
faculty_junction_id.bio: Maria is a member of various Advisory Boards - UK All-Party Parliamentary Group on AI (APPG AI) ,ORBIT and; SKEMA AI Institute, Vice Chair of techUK Data and AI leadership committee and member of BSI/ISO and; IEEE AI standard groups. She is also a passionate advocate for children rights in the age of AI, serving as member of the Advisory Board for UNICEF #AI4Children and World Economic Forum Generation AI programmes. At PwC, Maria manages the company’s efforts in deploying responsible AI and data across the UK business, its operations and clients.
faculty_junction_id.short_bio: Maria is a globally recognised, award winning AI ethics expert, public policy contributor.

faculty_id.title: The Ethical Implications of Technology on Humanity
faculty_id.description: This module unpacks the evolution of artificial intelligence and how it relates to human intelligence. It explores what 'work' might look like for humans in a future where AI becomes increasingly abundant, by touching upon the jobs and industries that might survive the fourth industrial revolution. The module highlights the skill sets that we will value in a post-automation world, makes suggestions for what potential solutions we may have for the problem of job displacement due to automation, and looks at how the Burning Man experiment demonstrates what humans might keep themselves busy with in a post-AI, post-automation world.
faculty_id.short_description: This module unpacks the evolution of artificial intelligence and how it relates to human intelligence.

faculty_junction_id.name: Tannya Jajal
faculty_junction_id.title: Regional Resource Manager
faculty_junction_id.bio: She has spoken at 40+ events to represent her views on future technology, the future of work, and the ethics of artificial intelligence. Tannya encourages current and future leaders to explore the ethical and practical implications of exponential technologies on business, life and society at large. She is an advocate of radical innovation, the rise of meaningful work and skills in a post-automation world, and a proponent of educational reform. Tannya is a Regional Resource Manager at VMware, a market leader in hybrid cloud solutions, leading the way forward for digital transformation.
faculty_junction_id.short_bio: Tannya is a keynote speaker, futurist, and author of the upcoming book, "Thinking Machines: A.I. and the Intelligence Explosion".

faculty_id.title: AI and Nigeria: Exploring Threats to Human Rights
faculty_id.description: This module looks at the implications of artificial intelligence technologies on human rights in Nigeria. The lecture begins with an explanation of AI and human rights before moving into specific use cases of AI technology in Nigeria and the effects that they have had on society. The course summarizes key considerations that must be taken into account to develop equitable and just AI systems, and concludes with an important note on inclusion in the AI ecosystem.
faculty_id.short_description: This module looks at the implications of artificial intelligence technologies on human rights in Nigeria.

faculty_junction_id.name: Favour Borokini
faculty_junction_id.title: Data and Digital Rights Researcher
faculty_junction_id.bio: Favour also works as a Content Writer with Ethical Intelligence, an AI Ethics consulting firm and with various research groups on topics related to data protection regulation and healthcare delivery. She is currently an Affiliate with The Future Society.
faculty_junction_id.short_bio: Favour is a Data and Digital Rights Researcher at Pollicy Uganda working remotely from Nigeria. In her role at Pollicy, she arches a number of knotty topics related to technology-facilitated violence against women and the general impact of subsisting and emerging technologies on social justice and equality.

faculty_id.title: The Role of Culture in AI Ethics: An Eastern Perspective
faculty_id.description: This module analyzes the shortcomings of the present AI ethics discourse and discusses the importance of cultural perspectives in AI Ethics through the lens of Eastern cultural and philosophical approaches. Using examples from South Korea, China, Japan and Buddhist philosophy, we explore the inherent links between culture and ethics, and seek to understand the value of nuanced approaches to global AI ethics frameworks.
faculty_id.short_description: This module analyzes the shortcomings of the present AI ethics discourse and discusses the importance of cultural perspectives in AI Ethics.

faculty_junction_id.name: Jibu Elias
faculty_junction_id.title: Content and Research Head
faculty_junction_id.bio: Jibu is also a member of the OECD Network of Experts on AI (ONE AI) and one of the founding Editorial Board Members of Springer’s AI and Ethics journal, the first multidisciplinary academic journal on AI ethics. With years of experience covering emerging technologies with PC Mag and the Times of India Group, Jibu’s work currently focuses on building a unified AI ecosystem in India. He is an alumnus of The London School of Economics, where he studied International Relations, specializing in Sino-India relations.
faculty_junction_id.short_bio: Jibu Elias is an AI Ethicist, Researcher, and the leading expert on India’s AI ecosystem and is the Research & Content Lead at INDIAai -The National AI Portal for the Government of India.

faculty_id.title: A Cybernetics Approach to Ethical AI Design
faculty_id.description: Cybernetics and artificial intelligence share a long, intertwined history. This module explores the relationship between cybernetics and AI ethics, and looks at how cybernetics can be leveraged to reframe how we think about and how we undertake ethical AI design. The module is divided into three sections, beginning with an introduction to cybernetics. Following that, we explore different ways of thinking about AI ethics, before concluding by bringing the two concepts together to understand a new approach to ethical AI design.
faculty_id.short_description: This module explores the relationship between cybernetics and AI ethics, and looks at how cybernetics can be leveraged to reframe how we think about and how we undertake ethical AI design.

faculty_junction_id.organization: School of Cybernetics (3A Institute), Australian National University
faculty_junction_id.name: Ellen Broad
faculty_junction_id.title: Associate Professor and Associate Director for Education
faculty_junction_id.bio: Ellen is a member of the Australian government's Data Advisory Council and author of “Made by Humans: the AI Condition” (Melbourne University Publishing, 2018). She has written about data for publications including The Guardian, New Scientist and Griffith Review. A board game about data she created with Jeni Tennison, CEO of the Open Data Institute, is being played in 19 countries.
faculty_junction_id.short_bio: Ellen Broad is an Associate Professor with the School of Cybernetics and Associate Director for Education. She is not sure how to describe her expertise anymore, having worked in roles spanning engineering, database design, data publication and maintenance, policy and law. Prior to joining 3AI, Ellen was technical lead for the Consumer Data Standards program within CSIRO's Data61, designing APIs and validation tools to support consumers sharing data safely with organisations of their choosing. She has also held roles including Head of Policy for the Open Data Institute (ODI), headquartered in London; ministerial adviser on data to senior UK cabinet minister Elisabeth Truss; and Manager of Digital Policy and Projects for the International Federation of Library Associations and Institutions, headquartered in the Netherlands.

faculty_id.title: An Ethics Model for Innovation: The PiE Model
faculty_id.description: How should organizations put AI ethics and responsible AI into practice? Is the answer AI ethics principles and AI ethics boards or should everyone developing AI systems become experts in ethics? In this module, Canca presents the model developed and employed at AI Ethics Lab: The Puzzle-solving in Ethics (PiE) Model. The PiE Model is a comprehensive and structured practice framework for organizations to integrate ethics into their operations as they develop and deploy AI systems. The PiE Model aims to make ethics a robust and integral part of innovation and enhance innovation through ethical puzzle-solving.
faculty_id.short_description: In this module, Canca presents the model developed and employed at AI Ethics Lab: The Puzzle-solving in Ethics (PiE) Model.

faculty_junction_id.name: Cansu Canca
faculty_junction_id.title: Founder and Director
faculty_junction_id.bio:
Cansu serves as an AI Ethics and Governance Expert consultant to the United Nations, working with UNICRI Centre for AI & Robotics and the Interpol in building a “Toolkit for Responsible AI Innovation in Law Enforcement”. Cansu has a Ph.D. in philosophy specializing in applied ethics. She primarily works on ethics of technology, having previously worked on ethics and health. She serves as an ethics expert in various ethics, advisory, and editorial boards.

Prior to AI Ethics Lab, she was on the full-time faculty at the University of Hong Kong, and an ethics researcher at the Harvard Law School, Harvard School of Public Health, Harvard Medical School, National University of Singapore, Osaka University, and the World Health Organization. She was listed among the “30 Influential Women Advancing AI in Boston” and the “100 Brilliant Women in AI Ethics”. She is also the first technology and AI ethicist in Turkey.
faculty_junction_id.short_bio: Cansu is a philosopher and the Founder and Director of AI Ethics Lab, where she leads teams of computer scientists, philosophers, and legal scholars to provide ethics analysis and guidance to researchers and practitioners. She is also the Ethics Lead and Research Associate Professor at the Institute for Experiential AI at Northeastern University, co-leading their Responsible AI practice.

faculty_id.title: Data Science against COVID-19: The Valencian Experience
faculty_id.description: In this module, we explore the ELLIS Alicante Foundation’s Data-Science for COVID-19 team’s work in the Valencian region of Spain. The team was founded in response to the pandemic in March 2020 to assist policymakers in making informed, evidence-based decisions. The team tackles four different work areas: modeling human mobility, building computational epidemiological models, predictive models on the prevalence of the disease, and operating one of the largest online citizen surveys related to COVID-19 in the world. This lecture explains the four work streams and shares lessons learned from their work at the intersection between data, AI, and the pandemic.
faculty_id.short_description: In this module, we explore the ELLIS Alicante Foundation’s Data-Science for COVID-19 team’s work in the Valencian region of Spain.

faculty_junction_id.name: Nuria Oliver
faculty_junction_id.title: Scientific Director and Co-Founder
faculty_junction_id.bio: Nuria is well known for her work in computational models of human behaviour, human computer-interaction, intelligent user interfaces, mobile computing and big data for social good. She is the named inventor of 41 patents, and a frequent keynote speaker both for technical and non-technical audiences. She regularly collaborates with and is featured by the media. She is very passionate about the power of technology to improve our quality of life, both individually and collectively. Nuria invests significant effort in outreach efforts to make technology more accessible to non technical audiences and to inspire young people – especially young women – to pursue careers in technology.
faculty_junction_id.short_bio: Nuria is a computer scientist. She holds a Ph.D. from the Media Lab at MIT. She is the first female computer scientist in Spain to be named an ACM Distinguished Scientist and an ACM Fellow. She is also a Fellow of the European Association of Artificial Intelligence and an IEEE Fellow. She is a member of the Academia Europaea and the fourth and youngest female member of the Spanish Royal Academy of Engineering.

faculty_id.title: What can religion contribute to the AI debate?
faculty_id.description: In this module, Bor considers the relationship between religion and AI, and religion’s possible contribution to the ethical AI debate. Using Judaism as a test case, Bor points to 7 core values that encapsulate key aspects of humanity. These values are: (1) Sanctity of the individual; (2) Virtue as foundation for knowledge; (3) Oneness and individuality; (4) Possibility of transformation; (5) Power of emotion; (6) Embodiment; and (7) Sacred time and space. By applying these values to questions around different innovations, Bor makes the case that religion can offer critical insights into how we develop and employ AI technologies in an ethical and responsible manner.
faculty_id.short_description: In this module, Bor considers the relationship between religion and AI, and religion’s possible contribution to the ethical AI debate.

faculty_junction_id.name: Harris Bor
faculty_junction_id.title: Barrister, Twenty Essex and Research Fellow
faculty_junction_id.bio: Harris is also a Research Fellow at the London School of Jewish Studies, and a rabbinic scholar with the Montefiore Endowment, London. His 2021 book “Staying Human: A Jewish Theology for the Age of Artificial Intelligence” (Cascade Books) applies approaches to oneness and difference found in the thought of philosophers Benedict Spinoza and Martin Heidegger to the challenges of religious belief and practice in the era of AI. Harris is also adviser to AI and Faith, a US cross-spectrum consortium of faith communities and academic institutions. He holds a Master of Laws in International and Comparative Dispute Resolution from Queen Mary, University of London, and a PhD in Theology from Cambridge University.
faculty_junction_id.short_bio: Harris Bor is a London barrister (trial advocate) specializing in international arbitration and commercial litigation, with a particular emphasis on corporate, joint venture, and fraud disputes.

faculty_id.title: Moral Agency in Artificial Intelligence: A Model for an Ongoing Discussion
faculty_id.description: How is artificial intelligence influencing the concept of moral agency? How is it potentially modifying the concept of moral responsibility? Who's responsible for what? In this module, Javier and José-Luis tackle these questions with the help of a simple moral agency model. Through a series of thought exercises, they argue that responsibility ought to rest solely with autonomous human actors, rather than with automatic machines. They make the case for responsibility as the core of ethics, and outline key questions that they feel will shape future ethical AI discussions.
faculty_id.short_description: How is artificial intelligence influencing the concept of moral agency? How is it potentially modifying the concept of moral responsibility?

faculty_junction_id.name: Javier Camacho Ibáñez
faculty_junction_id.title: Director of Ethical Sustainability
faculty_junction_id.bio: Javier has also developed a professional career in the IT and Telecom industry, and has provided consultancy services to several sectors for companies in different countries. He collaborates on several research projects on Artificial Intelligence and Business Ethics. He is a Member of the Chair of Business Ethics at that University, and a Member of Tech Committee: UNE -CTN 165 SC2 “Ethics and CSR”. He also provides Applied Ethics consultancy services at Sostenibilidad Etica.
faculty_junction_id.short_bio: Javier Camacho Ibáñez serves as the Director of Ethical Sustainability at ICADE, Comillas Pontifical University. He is also a teacher and a researcher in Business Ethics, AI Ethics and Corporate Governance. His current focus is on Ethics for AI from four different perspectives: purpose-driven applications and use cases; human-machine decision making interaction; algorithmic ethics; and overall impact.

faculty_id.title: Moral Agency in Artificial Intelligence: A Model for an Ongoing Discussion
faculty_id.description: How is artificial intelligence influencing the concept of moral agency? How is it potentially modifying the concept of moral responsibility? Who's responsible for what? In this module, Javier and José-Luis tackle these questions with the help of a simple moral agency model. Through a series of thought exercises, they argue that responsibility ought to rest solely with autonomous human actors, rather than with automatic machines. They make the case for responsibility as the core of ethics, and outline key questions that they feel will shape future ethical AI discussions.
faculty_id.short_description: How is artificial intelligence influencing the concept of moral agency? How is it potentially modifying the concept of moral responsibility?

faculty_junction_id.name: José Luis Fernández Fernández
faculty_junction_id.title: Professor
faculty_junction_id.bio:
From 2000 to 2003, he was Vice-Rector of External Relations and University Extension at the Comillas Pontifical University. For eleven years, he was Coordinator of Ethics of the Professions at the Universidad Pontificia Comillas ICAI-ICADE and General Coordinator of the Unijes Group of Ethics of the Professions. He has completed the CESCOM Compliance Certificate and is an accredited member of the ICCP, International Federation of Compliance Associations (IFCA).

José Luis is also a Fellow of the Caux Round Table, and the Chairman of the Ethics and Social Responsibility Subcommittee (CTN 165 SC2) of the Spanish Association for Standardization (UNE). He was President of EBEN-Spain between 1993 and 2007. He has written several books and numerous articles on the ethical aspects of digitalization (Business Digital Ethics). José Luis holds a Doctorate in Philosophy (PhD) from the Faculty of Philosophy of the Universidad Pontificia Comillas and an MBA from ICADE.
faculty_junction_id.short_bio: José Luis Fernández Fernández is a Professor at the Faculty of Economic and Business Sciences (ICADE) and Director of the Iberdrola Chair of Economic and Business Ethics.

faculty_id.title: AI Ethics and Hate Speech
faculty_id.description: This module explores the intersection between AI and hate speech in the context of the MENA region. Maha Jouini discusses how algorithms have exacerbated the challenge of hate speech, highlighting the role of social media platforms like Facebook and Twitter in further spreading harmful content. She goes on to explain the far reaching consequences of hate speech in the region, drawing on her years of work as an activist. The module concludes with an overview of potential solutions to the challenge, which offer lessons for actors engaged in building ethical AI systems across the world.
faculty_id.short_description: This module explores the intersection between AI and hate speech in the context of the MENA region.

faculty_junction_id.organization: African Center for Artificial Intelligence and Digital Technology
faculty_junction_id.name: Maha Jouini
faculty_junction_id.title: Founder
faculty_junction_id.bio:
Maha is a prominent advocate for youth and women’s rights, fighting against racism and gender-based violence. In 2018, Maghreb Voices named her their Personality of the Year for her work championing women’s rights. She is an author and blogger, using her platform to defend human rights in the MENA region. She has also published several articles on AI policies and the future of work in Africa. 

Maha is pursuing a PhD in Computer Science and Data Science. She holds a master’s degree in AI and emerging technologies from the Tianjin University of Education and Technology in China, where she spent many years living and working.
faculty_junction_id.short_bio: Maha Jouini is an expert in AI and emerging technologies based in Mauritania. She founded the African Center for Artificial Intelligence and Digital Technology in 2022 to support the adoption of AI policies across the African continent. Maha is a member of the Center for AI and Digital Policy’s (CAIDP) Fall 2022 AI Policy Clinic Research Group. She has also served as the North Africa Regional Director for the Africa Chamber of Digital Commerce since 2020, and was recently appointed an Ambassador for Cluster Digital Africa.

faculty_id.title: How Your Teeth, Your Smile and AI Ethics are Related
faculty_id.description: In this module, Maxime Ducret and Carl Mörch discuss the ethical implications of the use of AI technologies in the field of dentistry. While medical practices are generally carefully regulated, Ducret and Mörch find that there is little consideration for the ethical challenges currently present in applications of AI in the sector. They explain some of the potential repercussions of this gap and offer a framework of questions that practitioners can use to evaluate the ethical implications of their AI systems specific to this intersection of medicine and technology.
faculty_id.short_description: In this module, Maxime Ducret and Carl Mörch discuss the ethical implications of the use of AI technologies in the field of dentistry.

faculty_junction_id.organization: FARI - AI Institute for the Common Good
faculty_junction_id.name: Carl Mörch
faculty_junction_id.title: Co-Manager
faculty_junction_id.short_bio: Carl Mörch is co-manager of FARI – AI Institute for the Common Good, a research institute created by the Université Libre de Bruxelles (ULB) and the Vrijet Universiteit Brussel (VUB). He was a postdoctoral fellow at Algora Lab (Université de Montréal, Mila) in 2021, with the support of the International Observatory on the Societal Impacts of AI and Digital Technology (OBVIA). He is specialized in the responsible use of technologies, in particular in healthcare. He works on the ethical issues and social impact of AI and “Big Data”. He is also an adjunct professor in the Department of Psychology at the University of Québec in Montréal (UQAM).

faculty_junction_id.organization: University of Lyon, Faculty of Dentistry
faculty_junction_id.name: Maxime Ducret
faculty_junction_id.title: Dentist and Associate Professor
faculty_junction_id.short_bio: Maxime Ducret is a dentist and associate professor in Prosthetics and Digital Dentistry at the University of Lyon. He also serves as a Hospital Practitioner at the University Hospital of Lyon.

faculty_id.title: Ethics in AI for Peace
faculty_id.description: With rapid developments of data science, the greater availability of data and increased computer processing power, algorithms have become part of many spheres of our lives and work, including in peacebuilding and conflict prevention work. The “algo age” brought with it many technical, legal, and ethical questions that exceeded the scope of existing peacebuilding and peacetech ethics frameworks. This module raises awareness about these risks, and advises on how to apply tools to mitigate them by transferring ethical principles into practice to ensure that “AI ethics by design” is a first step and not an afterthought in AI for peace projects’ development and implementation.
faculty_id.short_description: How is AI being leveraged in the peacetech ecosystem? How can its applications be better aligned to ethical AI principles?

faculty_junction_id.name: Branka Panic
faculty_junction_id.title: Founder and Executive Director
faculty_junction_id.bio:
Branka is a passionate advocate for positive peace with 13 years of global experience in the humanitarian, peace, and development fields. She is a co-founder and board member of the Center for Exponential Technologies, as well as a member of the IEEE Global Initiative on Ethics of Autonomous and Intelligent Systems Working Group on Power and Technology.  

Branka holds a master’s in International Development Policy from Duke University, Sanford School of Public Policy, and a master’s in International Security from the University of Belgrade. She also studied International Peace and Conflict Resolution at the University of North Carolina.
faculty_junction_id.short_bio: Branka Panic is the Founder and Executive Director of AI for Peace, a nonprofit that works to ensure that AI benefits peace, security and sustainable development. She is also currently a visiting scholar at the Center on International Cooperation at New York University. She is focusing her research on the utilization of data-driven approaches to peacebuilding and prevention, conflict early warning/early action, and designing the pathways to establishing a Peacebuilding Data Hub.

faculty_id.title: Data Protection & AI: The relation between ethical and legal approaches
faculty_id.description: This module contains an overview of the different legal and ethical approaches around the world, with a special focus on the key differences depending on their geography. It covers the evolution from data protection regulations, to AI initiatives and laws, and the beginning of a new era of “AI accountability”.
faculty_id.short_description: This module contains an overview of the different legal and ethical approaches around the world, with a special focus on the key differences depending on their geography.

faculty_junction_id.name: Adrian Gonzalez Sanchez
faculty_junction_id.title: Senior Cloud, Data & AI Specialist for Public Sector, Microsoft and Responsible AI Lead
faculty_junction_id.bio:
Adrian is also a lecturer for the École des Dirigéants at HEC Montreal, Concordia Continuing Education, and online courses for O'Reilly Media, Linux Foundation, ICTC, etc. He regularly collaborates with 2U / GetSmarter as a tutor and facilitator for MIT Sloan's AI and Blockchain and Harvard VPAL's Fintech Executive Training courses.

Adrian has previously worked as a senior consultant and product owner in AI and data science with CGI Canada and IVADO Labs, Head of Customer Success for Peritus.ai Canada, and other data-driven companies in Europe and Latin America.

His areas of expertise are artificial intelligence, ethics and responsible AI, big data and cloud-enabled systems, national AI strategies and regulations (including the new AI Act), telecommunications, and the Internet of Things.
faculty_junction_id.short_bio: Adrian Gonzalez Sanchez is a Senior Cloud, Data & AI Specialist for Public Sector at Microsoft, and an active member of the Spanish Observatory of Ethical AI (OdiseIA).

faculty_id.title: Ethics Applied to AI: A Matter of Cultures and Words
faculty_id.description: ‘AI ethics’ has become a highly debated topic. Yet, looking closely, it appears that despite the quantity of discussions on the subject, their quality remains poor. The narrative surrounding ‘AI ethics’ (we prefer ethics applied to AI - EA2AI) is henceforth repeated without questioning its relevance and its applicability across diverse cultural contexts. This lack of critical thinking has inevitably opened the door to norms entrepreneurs, mostly from the Global North, are shaping to promote and protect their own interests, introducing a cultural bias in the debate. This lecture aims to offer some critical insights to dive deeper into the intricacies of EA2AI and to stress the need for both awareness towards the ‘AI ethics’ narrative and serious consideration for cultural perspectives.
faculty_id.short_description: This lecture aims to offer some critical insights to dive deeper into the intricacies of EA2AI and to stress the need for both awareness towards the ‘AI ethics’ narrative and serious consideration for cultural perspectives.

faculty_junction_id.name: Emmanuel R. Goffi
faculty_junction_id.title: Co-Founder and Co-Director
faculty_junction_id.bio:
Emmanuel holds a PhD in Political Science from the Paris Institute of Political Studies (SciencesPo). He is a research member at the Centre Éthique, Langue, Communication et Numérique team at the Université Mohammed Premier in Oujda, Morocco; the CEST – Centro de Estudos Sociedade e Tecnologia, Universidade de São Paulo, Brazil; the Z-Inspection® Initiative in Frankfurt, Germany; and the Centre for Defence and Security Studies at the University of Manitoba, in Winnipeg, Canada. 

He has been lecturing in several institutions in France, Canada and Germany, and has written numerous pieces on ethics applied to artificial intelligence. Emmanuel is regularly invited to give talks and lectures, and to participate in expert meetings and boards worldwide. His research focuses on the development of artificial intelligence and its ethical dimensions through a multicultural approach.
faculty_junction_id.short_bio: Emmanuel R. Goffi is a philosopher of artificial intelligence. He is the co-director and co-founder of the Global AI Ethics Institute in Paris, and co-founder and senior associate of Ethiciens du numériques (Digital Ethicists).

faculty_id.title: AI Ethics: The Case for Including Animals
faculty_id.description: In this module, Singer and Tse examine the existing AI ethics narrative and find a distinct lack of consideration for animals in the current discourse. Drawing on numerous case studies from the field, they make the case for including animals in the AI ethics debate. They also review existing applications of AI on animals and identify the ways in which practitioners can incorporate considerations for animals in the development and implementation of ethical AI technologies.
faculty_id.short_description: In this module, Singer and Tse examine the existing AI ethics narrative and find a distinct lack of consideration for animals in the current discourse.

faculty_junction_id.organization: University Center for Human Values, Princeton University
faculty_junction_id.name: Peter Singer
faculty_junction_id.title: Ira W. DeCamp Professor of Bioethics
faculty_junction_id.bio:
Singer first became well-known internationally after the publication of Animal Liberation in 1975. Some of his other well-known books are: Practical Ethics, The Expanding Circle, How Are We to Live?, Rethinking Life and Death, Pushing Time Away, The Life You Can Save, The Point of View of the Universe (co-authored with Katarzyna de Lazari-Radek), Ethics in the Real World, and Why Vegan?  

In 2012, Singer was made a Companion of the Order of Australia, the nation’s highest civic honor.  He founded the charity The Life You Can Save and is a founding co-editor of the Journal of Controversial Ideas. In 2021, he was awarded the Berggruen Prize for Philosophy and Culture.
faculty_junction_id.short_bio: Peter Singer was born in Melbourne, Australia, in 1946, and educated at the University of Melbourne and the University of Oxford. After teaching in England, the United States and Australia, he has, since 1999, been Ira W. DeCamp Professor of Bioethics in the University Center for Human Values at Princeton University.

faculty_junction_id.organization: University Center for Human Values, Princeton University
faculty_junction_id.name: Yip Fai Tse
faculty_junction_id.title: Research Assistant
faculty_junction_id.short_bio: Tse Yip Fai is a research assistant for Professor Peter Singer at Princeton University. He is researching the impact and ethics of artificial intelligence on nonhuman animals. Fai holds a degree in Chemistry from the Chinese University of Hong Kong, and one in Banking and Finance from the University of London. He is a 2021 Foresight Fellow in Animal Ethics For Artificial Intelligence. He was previously the China Strategy Consultant for Mercy For Animals, responsible for research and strategy for their expansion plans in China and Asia.

faculty_id.title: AI’s Interference with the Judicial Process and Governance Approaches to Regulate AI
faculty_id.description: This module contains two parts. The first half of the lecture aims to examine the impact of AI on the judicial process and on an accused’s due process rights. Specifically, it will look at how predictive algorithms are used in the criminal justice system and debate whether the use of such algorithms improve or worsen the fairness of the criminal process. In the second half of the lecture, a cross-cultural examination is conducted to see how AI governance initiatives in Europe and China seek to regulate the complex challenges posed by AI technologies.
faculty_id.short_description: This module explores the challenges of predictive algorithms on the criminal justice system and looks at diverse governance approaches to mitigate these challenges.

faculty_junction_id.name: Jane Loo
faculty_junction_id.title: Senior Research Associate and Adjunct Faculty
faculty_junction_id.short_bio: Jane Loo is a senior research associate and adjunct faculty at Singapore Management University. Her research interests include examining how technology influences the criminal process, the rule of law, and the respect for fundamental rights and liberties. Jane is currently teaching a module on AI, Law, and Ethics which embarks on an investigation into some prevalent ethical and legal challenges that arise out of the application of contemporary technologies in society.

faculty_junction_id.title: Research Associate
faculty_junction_id.short_bio: Willow Wong is a research associate at the Centre for AI and Data Governance, Singapore Management University. Her research interests are in moral philosophy, ethics and the philosophy of technology. Willow was recently appointed to the position of Adjunct Faculty at the Yong Pung How School of Law and enjoys teaching AI, Law, and Ethics with Jane Loo.

faculty_id.title: Data Theatre
faculty_id.description: The module names and describes the phenomenon of a 'data theatre' which has three elements, an aspect of a data injustice, a data silence, and a data violence. Through the use of a case study of ratings in platform work, De Souza describes how often while data is touted to be objective and neutral to give us a clear, and fair understanding of a phenomenon, we instead only see a performance of these attributes. The module offers some insights into how to recognize this phenomenon, as well as how to challenge its emergence.
faculty_id.short_description: This module names and describes the phenomenon of a 'data theatre' which has three elements, an aspect of a data injustice, a data silence, and a data violence.

faculty_junction_id.organization: Tilburg Institute for Law, Technology and Society
faculty_junction_id.name: Siddharth Peter de Souza
faculty_junction_id.title: Postdoctoral Researcher - Global Data Justice Project
faculty_junction_id.bio:
Prior to joining TILT, Siddharth was a PhD researcher at the Humboldt University of Berlin. He studied law at the University of Cambridge and the University of Delhi. He previously worked as a German Chancellor Fellow at the Max Planck Foundation for International Peace and Rule of Law, Heidelberg and as a judicial clerk at the High Court of Delhi. 

Siddharth is the founder of Justice Adda, a law and design social venture which develops innovative legal content to make the law accessible, useful and usable in India. He is also the co-founder of d-Van, a design thinking transformations lab based in India.
faculty_junction_id.short_bio: Siddharth Peter de Souza is a postdoctoral researcher for the Global Data Justice project at the Tilburg Institute for Law, Technology and Society (TILT). He is interested in the role data plays at the intersection of law and development.

faculty_id.title: The Islamic Philosophy of Techno-Social Good
faculty_id.description: In this module, Amana Raquib will situate and contextualize the ethical discourse around AI within the larger nexus of technology, society and ethics. Looking at the potential of technology both as an expression of human creativity, and as a means for enabling different visions and versions of societies and individuals that can be shaped through various ethical models informing the technological design and development. On the one hand, she will evaluate the ethical and moral dilemmas through evaluating the overall meaningfulness behind the creation and use of technologies, especially AI, in a late-modern age. She’ll then apply the Islamic ethical standards of human well-being (maslaha) and the eventual objective of attaining excellence of human character along with the traditional Islamic hierarchy of necessities, needs and enhancements to look at the role of AI in human life.
faculty_id.short_description: In this module, Amana Raquib will situate and contextualize the ethical discourse around AI within the larger nexus of technology, society and ethics.

faculty_junction_id.name: Amana Raquib
faculty_junction_id.title: Assistant Professor of Religion and Philosophy, Department of Social Sciences and Liberal Arts
faculty_junction_id.bio: Amana’s areas of research include: Islamic theology and ethics, philosophy of technology, entrepreneurship from an Islamic perspective, Islamic ethics of environment, and the intersection of Islamic theology with the philosophy of science. She has been interviewed by Wired magazine, and has appeared as a guest on the Tech on Earth podcast series by the Notre Dame-IBM Tech Ethics Lab.
faculty_junction_id.short_bio: Amana Raquib is an Assistant Professor of Religion and Philosophy in the Department of Social Sciences and Liberal Arts at the Institute of Business Administration, Karachi. She is the author of the book Islamic Ethics of Technology: An Objectives’ Approach. She is also the co-recipient of a Facebook research grant under their Ethics in AI Research Initiative for the Asia Pacific for her project titled “Culturally informed pro-social AI regulation and persuasion framework”.

faculty_id.title: Trustworthy Cities: Ethical Urban Artificial Intelligence
faculty_id.description: This module explains how cities are increasingly embracing the use of algorithmic tools to address all sorts of urban challenges and improve the provision of public services. It also discusses the ethical implications of the use of artificial intelligence in urban contexts and, building on the research of the Global Observatory of Urban Artificial Intelligence, it provides an overview of some of the initiatives and ethical principles promoted by cities.
faculty_id.short_description: This module explains how cities are increasingly embracing the use of algorithmic tools to address all sorts of urban challenges and improve the provision of public services.

faculty_junction_id.name: Marta Galceran
faculty_junction_id.title: Research Fellow - Global Cities Programme
faculty_junction_id.bio: Marta also leads the research at the Global Observatory of Urban Artificial Intelligence (GOUAI), within the Cities Coalition for Digital Rights. Before joining CIDOB, she held the position of Program Coordinator of the Smart City Expo World Congress and senior consultant at Anteverti, where she advised local governments and international organizations (i.e., UN-Habitat, IADB, European Commission) on internationalization and urban innovation policies. Marta holds an MA in International Relations from the University of Warwick and a BA in Political Sciences from Pompeu Fabra University.
faculty_junction_id.short_bio: Marta Galceran is a Research Fellow with the Global Cities Programme at CIDOB (Barcelona Centre for International Affairs), and a part-time lecturer on International Relations at Pompeu Fabra University and CEI-International Affairs. Her research focuses on city diplomacy, urban alliances and global governance, particularly in the field of digital transitions and technological humanism. She has authored several policy papers, academic articles, and other publications on these topics.

faculty_id.title: AI for Social Impact in the Global South
faculty_id.description: This lecture describes AI work carried out for social impact (AI4SI) in the developing world, at the Wadhwani Institute for Artificial Intelligence in India. We introduce what we mean by AI4SI, briefly describe how this work ties in to the UN Sustainable Development Goals, and the overall challenges in introducing and deploying AI technology for social upliftment in areas where technology adoption is limited, and AI is poorly understood. Finally, we describe three case studies of specific AI projects we are working on in the agriculture and healthcare domains, as well as challenges encountered in these projects at various stages of development, from data to adoption to deployment.
faculty_id.short_description: This lecture describes AI work carried out for social impact (AI4SI) in the developing world, at the Wadhwani Institute for Artificial Intelligence in India.

faculty_junction_id.organization: The Wadhwani Institute for Artificial Intelligence
faculty_junction_id.name: Alpan Raval
faculty_junction_id.title: Chief Scientist, AI/ML
faculty_junction_id.bio: Alpan is a physicist by training, with a PhD from the University of Maryland and an undergraduate degree from the Indian Institute of Technology, Kanpur. Before joining Wadhwani AI, he previously led applied AI teams at LinkedIn and Amazon, and worked as a researcher at D. E. Shaw Research. Earlier on, he taught mathematics and computational biology as a faculty member at the Claremont Colleges in California.
faculty_junction_id.short_bio: Alpan Raval is Chief Scientist, AI/ML at the Wadhwani Institute for Artificial Intelligence (Wadhwani AI), which is a non-profit institute in India developing AI for social impact in under-served communities across the Global South.

faculty_id.title: Global Pact: Birth and Organization of Territories
faculty_id.description: In this module, Polisena makes the case for the creation of a global pact to govern emerging technologies, especially AI and data based systems. Highlighting the value of lived experience in research, she points to the need for stronger governance measures around AI technologies that account for their impacts on humanity and the environment. Later in the lecture, Polisena explores how a global pact might transform society to mitigate some of the negative impacts of technology we are seeing today.
faculty_id.short_description: In this module, Polisena makes the case for the creation of a global pact to govern emerging technologies, especially AI and data based systems.

faculty_junction_id.name: Viviana Polisena
faculty_junction_id.title: Professor-Researcher
faculty_junction_id.bio: Her research interests include artificial intelligence, ethics, logic, philosophy, history and sociology of sciences. She holds a master’s degree in Human and Social Sciences from Paris-Sorbonne University and a diploma in the Philosophy of Physics from the Institute of Philosophy and Complexity Sciences (IFICC) in Chile. She is currently pursuing a doctorate of philosophy at the Pontifical Catholic University of Argentina (UCA). She is a member of the Global AI Ethics Consortium and a Fellowships Evaluation Expert at the European Commission.
faculty_junction_id.short_bio: Viviana Polisena is a Professor-Researcher at the Catholic University of Córdoba.

faculty_id.title: Artificial Intelligence and the African Philosophy of Ubuntu
faculty_id.description: In this lecture, Dorine van Norren explores the implications of Ubuntu philosophy on AI ethics. She begins with an overview of Ubuntu, explaining its central idea of “I am because we are”. She then looks at the COMEST principles, which informed the 2021 UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI, drawing comparisons between the Western or Global North’s approach to principles with that of the Ubuntu philosophy. Through this exercise, she makes the case for a more inclusive approach to AI ethics and raises key questions to guide future discourse in this space.
faculty_id.short_description: In this lecture, Dorine van Norren explores the implications of Ubuntu philosophy on AI ethics.

faculty_junction_id.organization: Van Vollenhoven Institute for Law, Governance and Society, Leiden University
faculty_junction_id.name: Dorine van Norren
faculty_junction_id.title: Associate Researcher
faculty_junction_id.bio: Dorine is a lawyer and a diplomat by profession. She has a master’s degree in international and Dutch law, as well as a PhD in law and development studies. Dorine studied law in Amsterdam, Cape Town and Lyon, and has lived and worked in Sri Lanka and Turkey. Her research looks at different world philosophies, sustainable development, and broader legal and well-being reform. Dorine is also a self-taught visual artist.
faculty_junction_id.short_bio: Dorine van Norren is an associate researcher at the Van Vollenhoven Institute for Law, Governance and Society at Leiden University. She also serves as a Strategic Advisor for Western Hemisphere (North and South America, the Caribbean) Affairs at the Dutch Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

faculty_id.title: Using AI Applications to Achieve Environmental Sustainability in North Africa
faculty_id.description:
In this module, Maha Jouini and Muhammad Mokhtar explore the ethical use of AI technologies to address climate change in North African countries. Looking at examples from Mauritania, Libya, Egypt and more, they highlight some of the challenges and contexts specific to the region before pointing to potential solutions. They conclude their module with a series of recommendations around implementing AI systems in the region, such as the use of ethical frameworks to promote inclusivity and protect vulnerable populations.
